title: Why a Tiny Waterway Is Causing a Giant Headache for the U.S.
summary: Imagine a water highway so narrow that at its tightest spot, it's just 21 miles wide—about the length of a marathon. That's the Strait of Hormuz, and every day, giant ships carrying one out of every five barrels of oil in the world squeeze through it. But right now, that highway is mostly empty. Why? Because Iran has hidden missiles and drones along its coast and can strike any ship that tries to pass. President Trump wants the strait fully open again, but experts say it's way harder than it sounds. Iran is a huge country—about one-third the size of the entire continental U.S.—and for decades, it has been getting ready for exactly this kind of fight. Jason Campbell, a former Pentagon official, says Iran's weapons are spread out in many small factories and its soldiers don't wait for orders from the capital. That makes it really tough to stop them with just bombs from the sky. "It's very difficult to envision any scenario where you could satisfactorily secure the Strait of Hormuz absent ground forces," Campbell says. That means the U.S. might need tens of thousands of soldiers on the ground in Iran, which could take months and cost a lot. Another idea is to have Navy ships escort oil tankers, like the U.S. did in the 1980s. But back then, the Navy had more ships, and Iran's weapons were less advanced. Today, Iran can launch swarms of drones and missiles, making escort missions much more dangerous. Trump says the strait is open and the U.S. is making progress, but Iran vows to fight back. With gas prices rising and elections coming up, this narrow strip of water is causing a very big problem.
why_it_matters: If gas prices keep rising, it could squeeze family budgets and even influence elections, showing how faraway conflicts can hit home.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz has been a global choke point for oil for decades. Any conflict there can cause fuel prices to shoot up around the world.
President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) and Iran have had tense relations, and the U.S. military has kept forces in the Persian Gulf for a long time.
Jason Campbell, a former Pentagon official who studied military strategy, says Iran’s hidden weapons make it very hard to control the strait without sending in ground troops.
Article_Structure: WHO: Iran, President Trump, Jason Campbell, and the U.S. Navy
WHAT: The Strait of Hormuz is mostly empty because Iran can attack ships, and the U.S. is finding it very difficult to secure the waterway
WHERE: The narrow Strait of Hormuz near Iran’s coast
WHY: Iran has hidden missiles and drones spread out all over the country, so airstrikes alone aren't enough—ground forces would be needed, which is risky and expensive

perspectives.description: Opening the strait would lower oil prices and help the world economy.
Using military force could start a bigger war that hurts many innocent people and costs a huge amount of money.
The tricky geography and Iran’s military tactics create a stalemate that is hard to solve without new ideas.
